title: Proof
body_md:
We first treat small condition numbers. If $0<q\le\frac15$, then $q<\rho<(1+\sqrt2)q<\frac12$ and
$|m|<1$, so $|\Delta|<(1+q)/2\le\frac35$ and $|\mathsf p_\pm|<\frac35$. The slacks of
the stationary spiral are nonnegative, and the change of the first gradient
contributes a deficit larger than $-|\mathsf p_\pm|(X+1)-|\Delta|^2/4>-\frac{99}{100}$,
while the extra coordinate supplies at least $(1-q^4)^2$; the margin is
$(1-1/625)^2-\frac{99}{100}>0$. For the minimizer pair, $|m+\Delta|<\frac85$, hence
$R_{0\star}>\frac{61}{100}$, while $|T_{\star0}|<q/2+\frac18\le\frac9{40}$. This covers
$1<\kappa\le\frac94$.

We now treat the remaining condition numbers. For $\kappa\ge2$, $q<\rho<2q$,
because $F(2q,q)=q^2(8q-4q^2-1)>0$ for $q\ge3-2\sqrt2$, and $F(\cdot,q)$ increases through
its unique positive zero. Hence $|m+\Delta|<(\rho+q^2)/(2q)<\frac32$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:startupslack} gives $R_{0\star}>\frac{11}{16}>\frac58>|T_{\star0}|$. For
$\rho\le1$, use $X\le1$ in \eqref{eq:startupslack}; the first row of
Table~\ref{tab:startup} gives $R\mp T\ge\mathsf c_\mp+\mathsf d-|\mathsf b_\mp|>0$. For
$1\le\rho\le\frac65$ write $\omega=\frac{2\pi}3+\vartheta$. The identity
$\sin\vartheta=-\sinh^2t/\{\cosh t(\sqrt3+\sqrt{4\cosh^2t-1})\}$, $t=\log\rho$, together
with $\log\rho\ge2(\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$, gives $|\vartheta|\le\epsilon(\rho)t$. For
$k=3j+r$ it follows that $|e^{3ij\vartheta}-1|\le\epsilon\log X$; since
$|\mathsf b_\mp|<1$ and $\log X\le X-1$, \eqref{eq:startupslack} is bounded below by
$P_r^\mp(X)$, which the second row makes positive for every $X\ge1$. For
$\rho\ge\frac65$, bound $\operatorname{Re}(\mathsf b_\mp Z)\ge-|\mathsf b_\mp|X$; the third row makes
the resulting quadratic in $X$ positive and increasing for $X\ge\rho^{10}$, and
the remaining nine cases are checked exactly. Finally $\rho_{\rm sp}(2)>\frac{33}{100}$ and
$\rho_*<\frac{1713}{1000}$ by exact polynomial signs, so the intervals cover
$\kappa\ge2$ and overlap the first case. Theorem~\ref{thm:interpolation} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalization} give the function in $\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^3)$.
head: environment

label: lem:lineargap
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lineargap}
There are $a>0$, $\delta_0>0$, and certificates \eqref{eq:strictcert} with lags at
most five at the exponents $t=T+\delta$, $0<\delta\le\delta_0$, whose coefficients are
bounded uniformly in $\delta$ and whose symbols satisfy
$\Phi_{T+\delta}\le-a\delta$ at every frequency.
head: environment
name: Linear gap

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t=T+\delta$ and $G=\cosh t$. Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} provides at this
$G$ the boundary certificate of the family containing $G$: weights $w(G)$ in
the simplex on $J\subset\{2,3,5\}$ with $\Phi_{G,u_V(t)}=-(G-c)Q\le0$ on $[-1,1]$.
Use the same weights at the actual point $(G,u_q(t))$. The terms with $C$
cancel, because $\sinh mt=U_{m-1}(G)\sinh t$ and $\sum_mw_m=1$, and the coefficients
$1$ and $w_m/U_{m-1}(G)$ are bounded by $1$. On each closed arc of the
classification $V$ is continuously differentiable with $|V'|<1$, and near
$T$ the exponents $t\in(T,T+\delta_0]$ lie on one arc. Hence there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $\theta_V<1$ with $|V'|\le \theta_V$ on $(T,T+\delta_0]$, and, since
$T-\log q=V(T)$,
\[
 (t-\log q)-V(t)=\int_T^t\bigl(1-V'(\tau)\bigr)d\tau\ge(1-\theta_V)\delta .
\]
On every arc $u_V\ge\frac12$ (Propositions~\ref{prop:p1}, \ref{prop:p5arc},
Theorem~\ref{thm:p2arc}, and $u=1-1/(2G)$ on the spiral). Since $\cosh\ge1$, the
mean value theorem gives $u_q-u_V\ge(1-\theta_V)\delta$, and
$u_q^2-u_V^2\ge2u_V(u_q-u_V)\ge(1-\theta_V)\delta$. Lemma~\ref{lem:dualfactor} yields
\[
 \Phi_{G,u_q}(c)\le\Phi_{G,u_V}(c)-(G-c)(u_q^2-u_V^2)\le-(G-c)(1-\theta_V)\delta
 \quad(-1\le c\le1).
\]
If $T\ne0$, take $\delta_0\le|T|/2$; then $|t|\ge|T|/2$, $G-c\ge\cosh(T/2)-1>0$, and the
claim holds with $a=(\cosh(T/2)-1)(1-\theta_V)$. If $T=0$, add the weights
$b\delta$ on both minimizer constraints $\bar g+C\ge0$ and $\bar g-C\ge0$; this adds $2b\delta g$
to the symbol and keeps the cancellation of $C$. Here $u_q(t)\ge u_q(0)=\frac12$.
On $c\ge\frac{19}{20}$, $1-c^2\le\frac18$ gives $g\le\frac18-\frac14=-\frac18$, so the new
symbol is at most $-\frac14b\delta$. On $c\le\frac{19}{20}$, $G-c\ge\frac1{20}$, and the
symbol is at most $-\delta\{\frac1{20}(1-\theta_V)-2b\}\le-\frac1{40}(1-\theta_V)\delta$ for
$b\le\frac1{80}(1-\theta_V)$. This gives the claim with $a=\min(b/4,(1-\theta_V)/40)$.
head: environment

label: lem:telescoping
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:telescoping}
Let $\mathcal B$ be a banded functional of width $D$ and offset $o$ with
$\chi(\mathcal B)=0$ and $\hat{\mathcal B}\le-\varepsilon$ on $[0,\pi]$ for some
$\varepsilon\ge0$, and let $0\le a_0\le D$. There are real numbers
$\varpi_0,\dots,\varpi_D$ and a banded functional $\mathcal U$ of width $D-1$ and
offset $o$, with $|\mathcal U|\le c_D(|\mathcal B|+\varepsilon)$ for a constant $c_D$
depending only on $D$, such that for all sequences in every real Hilbert space
and every $j$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:telescoping}
 \mathcal B_j=-\varepsilon\lVert f_{j+o+a_0}\rVert^2-\Bigl\|\sum_{a=0}^D\varpi_af_{j+o+a}\Bigr\|^2+\mathcal U_{j+1}-\mathcal U_j .
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Telescoping

title: Proof
body_md:
The even cosine polynomial $\mathcal P=-\hat{\mathcal B}-\varepsilon$ is nonnegative of
degree at most $D$. By the Fej\'er--Riesz theorem~\cite{GS},
$\mathcal P(\omega)=|\sum_a\varpi_ae^{ia\omega}|^2$ for a polynomial of degree at most
$D$. The zeros of $z^D\mathcal P$ are invariant under $z\mapsto\bar z$ and
$z\mapsto1/\bar z$; taking the zeros in the open unit disk and half of those on
the unit circle, with multiplicity, gives a set invariant under conjugation,
so the $\varpi_a$ can be taken real. Moreover
$\sum_a\varpi_a^2=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi\mathcal P\,d\omega=-\sum_ac_{aa}-\varepsilon\le|\mathcal B|$.
Let $\tilde c_{ab}=c_{ab}+\varpi_a\varpi_b$, and add $\varepsilon$ to $\tilde c_{a_0a_0}$. The
quadratic form with coefficients $\tilde c_{ab}$ has symbol
$\hat{\mathcal B}+\mathcal P+\varepsilon=0$. With $\mathsf g_e(l)=\langle f_l,f_{l+e}\rangle$,
$\mu_{0,a}=\tilde c_{aa}$ and $\mu_{e,a}=2\tilde c_{a,a+e}$ for $e\ge1$, this form equals
$\sum_{e=0}^D\sum_{a=0}^{D-e}\mu_{e,a}\mathsf g_e(j+o+a)$, and the zero symbol means
$\sum_a\mu_{e,a}=0$ for every $e$. Therefore
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \sum_a\mu_{e,a}\mathsf g_e(j+o+a)=\sum_a\mu_{e,a}\bigl\{\mathsf g_e(j+o+a)-\mathsf g_e(j+o)\bigr\}
 =\mathcal R^e_{j+1}-\mathcal R^e_j,\\
 \mathcal R^e_j=\sum_a\mu_{e,a}\sum_{r=0}^{a-1}\mathsf g_e(j+o+r).
 \end{gathered}
\]
In the same way, $\chi(\mathcal B)=0$ gives $\sum_ad_ah_{j+o+a}=\mathcal W_{j+1}-\mathcal W_j$
with $\mathcal W_j=\sum_ad_a\sum_{r=0}^{a-1}h_{j+o+r}$. The functional
$\mathcal U=\mathcal W+\sum_e\mathcal R^e$ uses only the indices $j+o,\dots,j+o+D-1$,
because $r+e\le D-1$ in $\mathcal R^e_j$. Rearranging gives
\eqref{eq:telescoping}, and the bound on $|\mathcal U|$ follows from
$|\tilde c_{ab}|\le2|\mathcal B|+\varepsilon$.
head: environment

label: lem:plateauclass
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:plateauclass}
Let $\mathcal G$ be a class of $H$-segments closed under restriction to
consecutive indices, and let $\Gamma_{\mathcal G}$ be defined as $\Gamma$, with the
supremum over $\mathcal G$. Assume that $\Gamma_{\mathcal G}(p)>0$ for every $p$ and
that $r=\lim_p\Gamma_{\mathcal G}(p)^{1/p}>0$. Then there is no banded functional
$\mathcal B$ at the exponent $\log r$ with $\chi(\mathcal B)=0$, $\hat{\mathcal B}<0$ on
$[0,\pi]$, and $\mathcal B_j\ge0$ whenever $\mathcal B_j$ lies inside a member of
$\mathcal G$.
head: environment
name: Plateau for classes of segments

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that such a functional exists. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ with
$\hat{\mathcal B}\le-\varepsilon$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:telescoping} with $a_0=0$.
Summing \eqref{eq:telescoping} over consecutive $j$ and using
$|\langle f_l,f_{l'}\rangle|\le\frac12(\lVert f_l\rVert^2+\lVert f_{l'}\rVert^2)$ and
$|h_l|\le\frac12\lVert f_l\rVert^2$ gives \eqref{eq:energy} for every member of $\mathcal G$,
with $b_k=\lVert f_k\rVert^2$, $K=\max(|\mathcal U|/\varepsilon,1)$ and any $w\ge D+|o|+1$. The
proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:plateau} uses the certificate only through
\eqref{eq:energy}, and the class of segments only through the definition of
$\Gamma$, closure under restriction and re-indexing, and
$\Gamma_{\mathcal G}(p)\ge r^p$, which follows from submultiplicativity.
Submultiplicativity holds because $S_{k+p}=0$ forces $\sigma_{k+p}=0$ by the
minimizer inequality, hence $S_l=0$ for all $l\ge k+p$. That proof therefore
applies to $\mathcal G$ and shows that its growth rate is strictly smaller than
$r$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:continuation
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Continuation

title: Proof
body_md:
Realize the Gram matrix of $Y$ by vectors $e_0,\dots,e_{H+1}$ and put
$\sigma_l=(e_{l+1}+q^2e_{l-1})/(2q)$ for $1\le l\le H$. These $H$ data points and
$(0,0,0)$ satisfy \eqref{eq:interpolation} pairwise, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:interpolation} gives $\psi\in\mathcal S$ with $\nabla\psi(e_l)=\sigma_l$ and
$\psi(e_l)=\psi_l$. For $l\ge H+1$ set $\sigma_l=\nabla\psi(e_l)$, $\psi_l=\psi(e_l)$
and $e_{l+1}=2q\sigma_l-q^2e_{l-1}$. All data lie on the graph of $\nabla\psi$, and the
necessity part of Theorem~\ref{thm:interpolation} gives every interpolation
inequality.
head: environment

label: lem:relaxedrate
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:relaxedrate}
There is $H_0\ge M_0+2$ such that $\rho_H=e^T$ for every $H\ge H_0$.
head: environment
name: Bounded memory preserves the rate

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal I_H$ be the set of exponents $t$ for which some pair is
$H$-feasible at $(t-\log q,t)$, and let $\mathcal I_\infty$ be the corresponding
set with all lags. By Lemma~\ref{lem:vmono}, $t\in\mathcal I_\infty$ if and only if
$|t-\log q|\le V(t)$, so $\max\mathcal I_\infty=T$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral}. The
minimizer constraint gives $|C|\le\bar g\le1$ and $\bar g\ge0$, and the latter
implies $|t-\log q|\le\operatorname{arsinh}1$ on $\mathcal I_H$. Weak compactness of
probability measures and continuity of $a_m,b_m,g$ in $(t,c)$ show that
$\mathcal I_H$ is compact. The sets are nonempty, since
$T\in\mathcal I_\infty\subset\mathcal I_H$, and they decrease in $H$. Let
$t_H=\max\mathcal I_H$, attained by an $H$-feasible pair $(\nu_H,C_H)$. A
subsequence of $(t_H,\nu_H,C_H)$ converges to a limit satisfying every
fixed-lag constraint, so $\lim_Ht_H\in\mathcal I_\infty$ and $t_H\downarrow T$. Choose
$H_0\ge M_0+2$ with $t_{H_0}<T+\delta_0$, where $\delta_0$ is the constant of
Lemma~\ref{lem:lineargap}.

Let $H\ge H_0$ and $T<t\le T+\delta_0$. Combining the constraints of an
$H$-feasible pair with the multipliers of Lemma~\ref{lem:lineargap} gives a
nonnegative number, in which $C$ cancels, equal to
$\int\Phi_t\,d\nu\le-a(t-T)<0$. Hence $t\notin\mathcal I_H$, and also $t\notin\mathcal I_H$ for
$t>T+\delta_0$, since then $t>t_H$. Suppose that $\rho_H>e^T$ and put
$t=\log\rho_H$. The separation argument in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(a), applied to the finite system with lags at
most $H$, gives a certificate \eqref{eq:strictcert} at $t$ with lags at most
$H$. Its functional $e^{-2jt}Z_j$ has zero charge and negative symbol, and it
is nonnegative whenever it lies inside an $H$-segment, because $Z_j$ is a
nonnegative combination of valid inequalities. Lemma~\ref{lem:plateauclass},
applied to the class of all $H$-segments, gives a contradiction. Hence
$\rho_H=e^T$.
head: environment

label: lem:prices
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Functionals above the rate

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Z_j$ be the combination of interpolation inequalities given by the
certificate of Lemma~\ref{lem:lineargap} at $t$. The banded functional
$\mathcal B_j=e^{-2jt}Z_j$ has offset $-1$, width $M_0+2$, charge zero and symbol
at most $-a\delta$, and $|\mathcal B|$ is bounded uniformly in $\delta$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:telescoping} with $\varepsilon=a\delta$ and $a_0=1$ gives a functional
$\mathcal U^\delta$ of offset $-1$ and width $M_0+1$, with $|\mathcal U^\delta|$ bounded
uniformly in $\delta$. Whenever $\mathcal B_j$ lies inside an $H$-segment,
$\mathcal B_j\ge0$, and \eqref{eq:telescoping} gives
$\mathcal U^\delta_{j+1}-\mathcal U^\delta_j\ge a\delta\lVert f_j\rVert^2$. Define
$\mathcal V_\delta(Y_k)=-a^{-1}e^{2(k-M_0)t}\,\mathcal U^\delta_{k-M_0}$. The functional
$\mathcal U^\delta_{k-M_0}$ uses the indices $k-M_0-1,\dots,k$, which belong to $Y_k$
since $H\ge M_0+2$; so $\mathcal V_\delta$ is a linear functional on $\mathcal E_H$ with
coefficients independent of $k$ and bounded uniformly in $\delta$. For
$H\le k\le n-2$, $\mathcal B_{k-M_0}$ uses the indices $k-M_0-1,\dots,k+1$ and lies
inside the segment, and $\mathcal U^\delta_{k-M_0+1}$ is read from $Y_{k+1}$;
multiplying the last inequality at $j=k-M_0$ by $a^{-1}e^{2(k-M_0)t}$ gives (i).
Iterating (i) along an infinite $H$-segment gives
$\mathcal V_\delta(Y_k)-e^{-2nt}\mathcal V_\delta(Y_{k+n})\ge\delta\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}e^{-2it}\lVert e_{k+i-M_0}\rVert^2$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:relaxedrate}, $\Gamma_H(p)\le K_\delta e^{p(T+\delta/2)}$ for all $p$
and some $K_\delta$, and with \eqref{eq:windowgrowth},
$e^{-2nt}|\mathcal V_\delta(Y_{k+n})|\le|\mathcal V_\delta|e^{-2nt}\operatorname{tr}Y_{k+n}\to0$, which
proves (ii). By Lemma~\ref{lem:continuation}, every element of $\mathcal K_H$ is a
window of an infinite $H$-segment, so $\mathcal V_\delta\ge0$ on $\mathcal K_H$.
head: environment

label: lem:exactprice
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: A functional at the exact rate

title: Proof
body_md:
By the uniform bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:prices}, there are $\delta_n\downarrow0$ such
that $\mathcal V_{\delta_n}$ converges to a linear functional $\mathcal V_*$. Properties
(a) and (b) follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:prices} in the limit. For (c), the
stationary sequence restricted to $l\ge0$ is an infinite $H$-segment with
$\lVert e_l\rVert^2=e^{2lT}$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:prices}(ii) gives
$\mathcal V_\delta(Y_k)\ge\delta\sum_{i\ge0}e^{-2i(T+\delta)}e^{2(k+i-M_0)T}
=\frac{\delta}{1-e^{-2\delta}}e^{2(k-M_0)T}\ge\frac12e^{2(k-M_0)T}$; the bound passes to
the limit.
head: environment

label: lem:kernel
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:kernel}
$\rho_{\mathcal N}<e^T$.
head: environment
name: A smaller rate on the kernel

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $\rho_{\mathcal N}\le\rho_H=e^T$. Suppose that $\rho_{\mathcal N}=e^T$. Fix
$(v,t)=(T-\log q,T)$, and let $Y^{\nu,C}$ be the window $Y_H$ of the stationary
sequence of $(\nu,C)$ at the exponent $T$. Its Gram entries are integrals of
continuous functions of $c$, and its values are affine in $C$ and
$\int\operatorname{Re} m\,d\nu$, for every pair $(\nu,C)$. Hence
$\mathcal V_*(Y^{\nu,C})=\int\vartheta\,d\nu+\vartheta_0C$ for a continuous function $\vartheta$
and a number $\vartheta_0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:exactprice}(c), no $H$-feasible pair
satisfies $\mathcal V_*(Y^{\nu,C})=0$. Write the inequalities of $H$-feasibility as
$\int\phi_i\,d\nu+\varsigma_iC\ge0$, $i\in\mathcal I$, and the equation as
$\int\vartheta\,d\nu+\vartheta_0C=0$. The set
\[
 \operatorname{conv}\{(\phi(c),\vartheta(c)):c\in[-1,1]\}+\mathbb R(\varsigma,\vartheta_0)-(\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal I}\times\{0\})
\]
is a compact convex set plus a finitely generated cone, hence closed and
convex, and it does not contain zero. Strict separation, as in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(a), gives nonnegative $\alpha_m,\beta_m$ $(m\le H)$
and $\gamma_\pm$, a real number $\zeta$, and $\varepsilon>0$ with
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Phi_{\mathcal N}(c)&=\sum_{m\le H}\bigl\{\alpha_m(a_m-b_m)+\beta_m(a_m+b_m)\bigr\}+(\gamma_++\gamma_-)g+\zeta\vartheta\le-\varepsilon,\\
 0&=\sum_{m\le H}(\alpha_m-\beta_m)\sinh mT+\gamma_+-\gamma_-+\zeta\vartheta_0 .
 \end{aligned}
\]
Form $Z_j$ from these multipliers as in Lemma~\ref{lem:energy}, and set
$\mathcal B_j=e^{-2jT}\{Z_j+\zeta\mathcal V_*(Y_{j+H})\}$. This is a banded functional at
the exponent $T$, of offset $-1$ and width $H+2$. On the stationary sequence
of any $(\nu,C)$, the identities \eqref{eq:waveslacks}, the linearity of
$\mathcal V_*$ and $Y_{j+H}=e^{2jT}Y_H$ give $\mathcal B_j=\int\Phi_{\mathcal N}\,d\nu$;
comparison with \eqref{eq:stationaryvalue} for $\nu=\delta_c$ and all $C\in\mathbb R$
yields $\chi(\mathcal B)=0$ and $\hat{\mathcal B}(\omega)=\Phi_{\mathcal N}(\cos\omega)\le-\varepsilon$.
If $\mathcal B_j$ lies inside an $\mathcal N$-segment, then $Z_j\ge0$ and
$Y_{j+H}\in\mathcal N$, so $\mathcal B_j\ge0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:plateauclass}, applied to the
class of $\mathcal N$-segments, gives a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:nearkernel
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:nearkernel}
There are an integer $p_*\ge H$ and a number $\eta>0$ such that, if an
$H$-segment and an index $k\ge H$ satisfy $k+p_*\le n-1$ and
$\mathcal V_*(Y_k)\le\eta\operatorname{tr}Y_k$, then
$\operatorname{tr}Y_{k+p_*}\le\frac12e^{2p_*T}\operatorname{tr}Y_k$.
head: environment
name: Contraction near the kernel

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $r$ with $\rho_{\mathcal N}<r<e^T$ and $K_r$ with $\Gamma_{\mathcal N}(p)\le K_rr^p$ for all
$p$. If $Y_k\in\mathcal N$, forward invariance shows that the restriction of the
segment to the indices $l\ge k-H$ is an $\mathcal N$-segment, and the argument
leading to \eqref{eq:windowgrowth}, with $\Gamma_{\mathcal N}$ in place of $\Gamma_H$,
gives for $p_*\ge H$
\[
 \operatorname{tr}Y_{k+p_*}\le(H+2)K_r^2\max(1,r)^{2(H+1)}r^{2(p_*-H)}\operatorname{tr}Y_k .
\]
Choose $p_*\ge H$ such that this coefficient is at most $\frac14e^{2p_*T}$. Suppose
that no $\eta>0$ has the stated property for this $p_*$. All conditions are
invariant under restriction, translation of indices, and multiplication of
all positions by a common factor and of all values by its square. Hence
there are $H$-segments of length $H+p_*+1$ with $\operatorname{tr}Y_H=1$,
$\mathcal V_*(Y_H)\to0$ and $\operatorname{tr}Y_{H+p_*}>\frac12e^{2p_*T}$. Record each of
them by the Gram matrix of $e_0,\dots,e_{H+p_*+1}$ and the values
$\psi_1,\dots,\psi_{H+p_*}$. These data form a closed convex cone, on which
$\operatorname{tr}Y_H=1$ bounds all entries, by $\lVert e_l\rVert^2\le1$ for $l\le H+1$,
$\lVert e_l\rVert\le\Gamma_H(l-H)$ for $l\ge H$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and
$|\psi_l|\le\lVert e_l\rVert^2/2$. A subsequence converges to the data of an
$H$-segment with $\operatorname{tr}Y_H=1$, $\mathcal V_*(Y_H)=0$ and
$\operatorname{tr}Y_{H+p_*}\ge\frac12e^{2p_*T}$. Its window $Y_H$ lies in $\mathcal N$, which
contradicts the first part.
head: environment

label: eq:constantwindow
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the upper bound in \eqref{eq:bounds}. Fix $H\ge H_0$, let $p_*$ and $\eta$ be as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:nearkernel}, and put $\mathsf A=|\mathcal V_*|/\eta$. By
\eqref{eq:windowgrowth} there is $\mathsf B\ge1$ with
$e^{-2pT}\operatorname{tr}Y_{k+p}\le\mathsf B\operatorname{tr}Y_k$ for $0\le p\le p_*$ and all
$H$-segments. We claim that every $H$-segment satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:constantwindow}
 \operatorname{tr}Y_l\le\mathsf B\max(1,\mathsf A\mathsf B)\,e^{2(l-k)T}\operatorname{tr}Y_k\quad(H\le k\le l\le n-1).
\end{equation}
Put $\tilde s_l=e^{-2(l-k)T}\operatorname{tr}Y_l$, and call $Y_l$ good if
$\mathcal V_*(Y_l)>\eta\operatorname{tr}Y_l$. For a good window,
Lemma~\ref{lem:exactprice}(b) gives
$\tilde s_l<\eta^{-1}e^{-2(l-k)T}\mathcal V_*(Y_l)\le\eta^{-1}\mathcal V_*(Y_k)\le\mathsf A\operatorname{tr}Y_k$.
For a window that is not good, Lemma~\ref{lem:nearkernel} gives
$\tilde s_{l+p_*}\le\frac12\tilde s_l$ whenever $l+p_*\le n-1$. Define $l_0=k$ and let
$l_{i+1}$ be $l_i+1$ or $l_i+p_*$ according as $Y_{l_i}$ is good or not, as long
as $l_{i+1}\le n-1$. By induction, $\tilde s_{l_i}\le\max(1,\mathsf A\mathsf B)\operatorname{tr}Y_k$
for every $i$: this holds for $i=0$; if $Y_{l_i}$ is good, then
$\tilde s_{l_i+1}\le\mathsf B\tilde s_{l_i}<\mathsf A\mathsf B\operatorname{tr}Y_k$; if not,
$\tilde s_{l_i+p_*}\le\frac12\tilde s_{l_i}$. Every $l\in[k,n-1]$ satisfies
$0\le l-l_i\le p_*$ for some $i$, and then $\tilde s_l\le\mathsf B\tilde s_{l_i}$. This
proves \eqref{eq:constantwindow}.

Now let $f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^d)$, let $e_k$ be the normalized errors with $e_{-1}=e_0$,
and shift the indices by one, $\hat e_l=e_{l-1}$, with gradients and values at
$\hat e_l$ for $l\ge1$. All these data lie on the graph of $\nabla\psi$, so they
form an infinite segment. Its window $\hat Y_H$ contains the positions
$e_{-1}=e_0,e_0,\dots,e_H$, and the comparison matrix gives
$\operatorname{tr}\hat Y_H\le c_H\lVert e_0\rVert^2$. For $N\ge H$, \eqref{eq:constantwindow}
gives
\[
 \lVert e_N\rVert^2=\lVert \hat e_{N+1}\rVert^2\le\operatorname{tr}\hat Y_N\le\mathsf B\max(1,\mathsf A\mathsf B)\,c_H\,e^{2(N-H)T}\lVert e_0\rVert^2 .
\]
The constants are independent of $f$, $d$ and $N$, and the comparison
matrix bounds the finitely many smaller $N$. This is the upper bound in
\eqref{eq:bounds}.

We now prove the lower bound. If $T\ne0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} give an optimal spectrum at $(T-\log q,T)$ with
at most two atoms and $|C|<\bar g$; if $T=0$, the three-cycle is a one-atom
spectrum. Lemma~\ref{lem:startup} gives $f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^{2r+1})$, $r\le2$, and $x_0$
with $\lVert x_N-x^\star\rVert\ge c\,e^{NT}\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert$ for all $N$. Adding
$\frac\mu2\lVert w\rVert^2$ in unused coordinates $w$, with $w_0=0$, embeds this example
in $\mathbb R^5$. Hence $c_\kappa\rho_{\rm HB}^N\le W_N^{(5)}$. The two bounds give the existence
of both limits in Theorem~\ref{thm:rate} and their common value $\rho_{\rm HB}$, and
\eqref{eq:spirallower} was proved above.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:p5local}, $V$ is even and analytic at $0$ with
$V(0)=\log\varphi$, so $V(t)=\log\varphi+O(t^2)$. The equation $T-V(T)=\log q$ has
derivative $1$ in $T$ at $T=0$, and the analytic implicit function theorem
gives $T=\log(q/q_c)+O(\log^2(q/q_c))$, $q_c=\varphi^{-1}$. Since
$d\log q/d\kappa=1/(\sqrt\kappa(\kappa-1))$ and
$\sqrt{\kappa_c}(\kappa_c-1)=\varphi^3(\varphi^6-1)=4\kappa_c$, exponentiation gives
\eqref{eq:critical}. As $q\downarrow0$, $T\to-\infty$ and $G\to\infty$, so the family
$P_1$ applies. Its regular system \eqref{eq:p1system}, \eqref{eq:p1blowup},
expanded at $z=0$ by equating coefficients, gives
$u_1=1-\frac z2+\frac{z^2}8-\frac{z^3}4+O(z^4)$ with $z=1/G=2\rho/(1+\rho^2)$. Inserting
this in $\rho/q=u+\sqrt{1+u^2}$, which is $u=\sinh(\log(\rho/q))$, and expanding at

$q=1$, $F(\rho,1)=(\rho-1)^2(\rho^2+1)-2=\rho^4-2\rho^3+2\rho^2-2\rho-1$ has a unique
positive root $\rho_*$, at which $F_\rho>0$, so $\rho_{\rm HB}=\rho_{\rm sp}\to\rho_*$.

label: lem:dominant
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:dominant}
Suppose $\rho_{\rm q}>\sqrt\beta$. If $\rho_a\ge\rho_b$, the roots of $a$ are real and
$\rho_a$ is a positive root of $a$. If $\rho_b\ge\rho_a$, the roots of $b$ are
real and distinct, $-\rho_b$ is a root of $b$, and the other root is
$-\beta/\rho_b\in(-\rho_b,0]$.
head: environment
name: Dominant quadratic roots

title: Proof
body_md:
For $p\in\mathbb R$ the largest root modulus of $z^2-pz+\beta$ equals $\sqrt\beta$ if
$p^2\le4\beta$ and $(|p|+\sqrt{p^2-4\beta})/2>\sqrt\beta$ otherwise; on
$|p|>2\sqrt\beta$ it is strictly increasing in $|p|$. Put
$p_a=1+\beta-x>p_b=1+\beta-y$. If $\rho_a\ge\rho_b$, then $\rho_a=\rho_{\rm q}>\sqrt\beta$
and $|p_a|>2\sqrt\beta$; if $p_a\le0$, then $|p_b|>|p_a|$ and $\rho_b>\rho_a$, a
contradiction, so $p_a>0$ and the largest root $(p_a+\sqrt{p_a^2-4\beta})/2=\rho_a$
is positive. If $\rho_b\ge\rho_a$, then $|p_b|>2\sqrt\beta$; if $p_b\ge0$, then
$|p_a|>|p_b|$ and $\rho_a>\rho_b$, a contradiction. So $p_b<0$, the roots
$(p_b\mp\sqrt{p_b^2-4\beta})/2$ are real and distinct, the first equals $-\rho_b$,
and the product of the roots is $\beta$.

title: Proof
body_md:
At $|z|=1$, $z+\beta/z=(1+\beta)\cos\omega+i(1-\beta)\sin\omega$, so
$s=(1-\beta)\sin\omega/B>0$ on $(0,\pi)$ and $g-2is$ lies in the open lower half
plane. By \eqref{eq:factor},
$g-2is=|g-2is|\,e^{i(\pi+\arg a-\arg b)}$, and
$\pi+\arg a-\arg b\equiv-\arg\bigl(b/(-a)\bigr)$; hence
$g-2is=|g-2is|e^{-i\Theta}$ with $\Theta\in(0,\pi)$, and $\cot\Theta=g/(2s)$. The
identity $g\sin\omega=2s\,\Xi(\cos\omega)$ is a polynomial identity in
$\cos\omega$, which gives \eqref{eq:Xi}. The leading coefficient of $\Xi$ is
$-4\beta/(2B(1-\beta))\le0$, so $\Xi$ is concave. Further
\[
 \Xi(1)=\frac{B^2-(1+\beta-A)^2}{2B(1-\beta)},\quad
 \Xi(-1)=\frac{B^2-(1+\beta+A)^2}{2B(1-\beta)} .
\]
Here $1+\beta-A=\alpha(L+\mu)/2>B$, and $1+\beta+A>B$ is equivalent to
$\alpha L<2(1+\beta)$; so $\Xi(\pm1)<0$. As $\omega\to0$ or $\omega\to\pi$,
$\cot\Theta=\Xi(\cos\omega)/\sin\omega\to-\infty$, so $\Theta\to\pi$. At $\omega=\pi$,
$a(-1)=2+2\beta-x>0$ and $b(-1)=2+2\beta-y>0$, so $b/(-a)<0$ and $\Theta(\pi)=\pi$.

label: lem:cubic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cubic}
For $r>0$ and $c=\cos\omega$,
\begin{align*}
H_r(c)={}&-4\beta r^3c^3-2r^2\bigl(r^2y-r^2-\beta r^2+\beta x-3\beta-\beta^2\bigr)c^2\\
&-r\bigl(r^4+r^2xy-2r^2x-2r^2y+3r^2+\beta^2r^2+3\beta^2\\
&\quad-\beta r^2x-\beta r^2y+2\beta r^2-\beta x-\beta y+2\beta\bigr)c\\
&+r^4(1+y-x)+r^2(1-x)(1-y)-2\beta r^2y+\beta^2r^2+\beta^2 .
\end{align*}
At $r=1$, $H_1(c)=(1-c)\mathcal L(c)$ with $\mathcal L$ as in \eqref{eq:E},
$\mathcal L(-1)=(2+2\beta-x)(2+2\beta-y)>0$ and $\mathcal L(1)=2(1-\beta)(y-x)+xy>0$. For
$\omega\in(0,\pi]$, $\Theta(\omega)>\omega/2$ if and only if $\mathcal L(\cos\omega)>0$.
Finally, with $\kappa'=\mu/L=x/y$, the identity \eqref{eq:gtd} holds.
head: environment
name: The lag-one cubic

title: Proof
body_md:
The formula for $H_r$, the factorization of $H_1$, the second expression for
$\mathcal L$ in \eqref{eq:E}, the endpoint values, and \eqref{eq:gtd} are polynomial
identities in $(c,r,x,y,\beta)$; for \eqref{eq:gtd} both sides equal
$x^2-2\beta x+2cx-2\kappa'x+2\kappa'\beta cx+2\kappa'(1-c)(1+\beta^2-2\beta c)$. For
$\omega\in(0,\pi)$ both $\Theta(\omega)$ and $\omega/2$ lie in $(0,\pi)$, where $\cot$
decreases, so $\Theta>\omega/2$ if and only if
$\Xi(c)/\sin\omega<\cot(\omega/2)=(1+c)/\sin\omega$, that is, $\mathcal L(c)>0$ by
\eqref{eq:E}. At $\omega=\pi$, $\Theta=\pi>\pi/2$ and $\mathcal L(-1)>0$.
head: environment

label: lem:iqc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:iqc}
There is a $2\times2$ Hermitian matrix $\Pi(\omega)$ of trigonometric
polynomials with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\par\hangindent 40\p@ For every $\psi\in\mathcal S$ and every sequence with $\tilde e\in\ell_2$,
\[
 \mathcal J(\tilde e,\tilde\sigma):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
 \begin{bmatrix}\hat e(\omega)\\\hat\sigma(\omega)\end{bmatrix}^*\Pi(\omega)
 \begin{bmatrix}\hat e(\omega)\\\hat\sigma(\omega)\end{bmatrix}d\omega\ \ge0,
\]
where $\hat e$ and $\hat\sigma$ are the Fourier transforms of $\tilde e$ and
$\tilde\sigma$, and $\Pi(\omega)$ acts blockwise.
\par\hangindent 40\p@ $[1;m]^*\Pi(\omega)[1;m]=\Phi_t(\omega)$, where $m=m(t,\omega)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: The certificate as an integral quadratic constraint

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the absolutely convergent sum
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal J'=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\Bigl[&\sum_{n\le M'}2\varrho^{-2k-n}\bigl(\alpha_n(R+T)_{k,k+n}+\beta_n(R-T)_{k,k+n}\bigr)\\
 &+4\varrho^{-2k}\bigl(\gamma_+(R+T)_{\star k}+\gamma_-(R-T)_{\star k}\bigr)\Bigr],
 \end{aligned}
\]
with $(R\pm T)_{\star k}=R_{k\star}\pm T_{\star k}$. Every point $e_k$, including
$e_k=0$ for $k<0$, lies on the graph of $\nabla\psi$, so every bracket is a
nonnegative combination of the inequalities of
Theorem~\ref{thm:interpolation}, and $\mathcal J'\ge0$. The sum converges absolutely
because $|\psi(e)|\le\frac12\lVert e\rVert^2$, $\lVert \nabla\psi(e)\rVert\le\lVert e\rVert$, and
$\varrho^{-2k-n}\lVert e_k\rVert\lVert e_{k+n}\rVert\le\frac12(\varrho^{-n}\lVert \tilde e_k\rVert^2+\varrho^n\lVert \tilde e_{k+n}\rVert^2)$.
The function values enter $\mathcal J'$ through
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\sum_k\Bigl[\sum_n2(\alpha_n-\beta_n)\bigl(\varrho^n\tilde\psi_{k+n}-\varrho^{-n}\tilde\psi_k\bigr)+4(\gamma_+-\gamma_-)\tilde\psi_k\Bigr]\\
 &\quad=4\Bigl[\sum_n(\alpha_n-\beta_n)\sinh nt+\gamma_+-\gamma_-\Bigr]\sum_k\tilde\psi_k=0 .
 \end{aligned}
\]
The remaining terms are quadratic in $(\tilde e,\tilde\sigma)$ with coefficients that
depend only on the differences of indices; for instance
$\varrho^{-2k-n}\lVert e_k-e_{k+n}\rVert^2=\lVert \varrho^{-n/2}\tilde e_k-\varrho^{n/2}\tilde e_{k+n}\rVert^2$ and
$\varrho^{-2k-n}\langle \sigma_k+\sigma_{k+n},e_{k+n}-e_k\rangle=
\langle \varrho^{-n/2}\tilde\sigma_k+\varrho^{n/2}\tilde\sigma_{k+n},\varrho^{n/2}\tilde e_{k+n}-\varrho^{-n/2}\tilde e_k\rangle$.
Write this quadratic form as $\sum_k\sum_{a,b}\langle \xi_{k+a},\mathsf Q_{ab}\,\xi_{k+b}\rangle$ with
$\xi_l=(\tilde e_l,\tilde\sigma_l)$ and real $2\times2$ blocks $\mathsf Q_{ab}=\mathsf Q_{ba}^{\mathsf T}$,
and put $\Pi(\omega)=\sum_{a,b}\mathsf Q_{ab}e^{i(b-a)\omega}$. Parseval's identity gives
$\mathcal J'=\mathcal J(\tilde e,\tilde\sigma)$, which is (a). For (b), evaluate the
per-step value of the quadratic form on the planar sequence
$\xi_l=(e^{il\omega},m\,e^{il\omega})$, that is, on the wave $e_l=z^l$, $\sigma_l=mz^l$,
$z=e^{t+i\omega}$; this value is $[1;m]^*\Pi(\omega)[1;m]$. By the computation in the
proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:spectralinterp}, with function values $\mathsf h e^{2lt}$, the
per-step value of the full bracket is
$\sum_n\{\alpha_n(a_n-b_n+C\sinh nt)+\beta_n(a_n+b_n-C\sinh nt)\}+\gamma_+(g+C)+\gamma_-(g-C)$
with $C=4\mathsf h-2\operatorname{Re} m$. Its function-value part is a multiple of the
cancelling sum above, so it vanishes, and the value is $\Phi_t(\omega)$ for every
$\mathsf h$.
head: environment

label: lem:homotopy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:homotopy}
Let $\mathcal G$ be the causal convolution operator on $\ell_2(\mathbb Z_{\ge0};\mathbb R^d)$ of a
stable, strictly proper rational transfer function $G$, and let $\Delta$ be a
causal map on sequences with $\lVert P_N\Delta\xi\rVert\le\lVert P_N\xi\rVert$ and
$\lVert P_N\Delta\xi-P_N\Delta\xi'\rVert\le\lVert P_N(\xi-\xi')\rVert$ for every $N$, where $P_N$
truncates to the indices $<N$, and with $\Delta0=0$. Let $\Pi$ be a bounded
Hermitian matrix function such that
$\mathcal J(\xi,\tau\Delta\xi)\ge0$ for all $\xi\in\ell_2$ and $\tau\in[0,1]$, with
$\mathcal J$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:iqc}, and
\[
 [G(e^{i\omega});1]^*\Pi(\omega)[G(e^{i\omega});1]\le-\varepsilon<0\quad(\omega\in[-\pi,\pi]).
\]
Then there is $c_*$ such that for all $\tau\in[0,1]$ and $f\in\ell_2$ the solution
$\xi$ of $\xi=\mathcal G\tau\Delta\xi+f$ satisfies $\lVert \xi\rVert\le c_*\lVert f\rVert$.
head: environment
name: Homotopy

title: Proof
body_md:
The loop is explicit, since $G$ is strictly proper: $\xi_k$ is determined by
$f_k$ and $\xi_0,\dots,\xi_{k-1}$, so the solution exists, is unique, and depends
causally on $f$. First, an a priori bound. If $\xi\in\ell_2$ solves the loop, then
$\zeta=\tau\Delta\xi\in\ell_2$, $\lVert \zeta\rVert\le\lVert \xi\rVert$, and $\xi=\mathcal G\zeta+f$. By the
frequency inequality, $\mathcal J(\mathcal G\zeta,\zeta)\le-\varepsilon\lVert \zeta\rVert^2$. The difference
$\mathcal J(\mathcal G\zeta+f,\zeta)-\mathcal J(\mathcal G\zeta,\zeta)$ is at most
$c_1\lVert f\rVert\lVert \zeta\rVert+c_2\lVert f\rVert^2$, with $c_1,c_2$ depending on $\sup\lVert \Pi\rVert$ and
$\sup|G|$. Since $\mathcal J(\xi,\zeta)\ge0$,
$\varepsilon\lVert \zeta\rVert^2\le c_1\lVert f\rVert\lVert \zeta\rVert+c_2\lVert f\rVert^2$, so $\lVert \zeta\rVert\le c_3\lVert f\rVert$ and
$\lVert \xi\rVert\le(\sup|G|\,c_3+1)\lVert f\rVert=:c_*\lVert f\rVert$, with $c_*$ independent of $\tau$.

Second, continuation in $\tau$. Suppose that for some $\tau$ every solution
with $f\in\ell_2$ lies in $\ell_2$, and let $|\tau'-\tau|\le1/(2c_*\sup|G|)$. Let $\xi'$
solve the loop with $\tau'$ and $f\in\ell_2$. For $N\ge0$, let $f_N$ be the
truncation $P_N\{f+\mathcal G(\tau'-\tau)\Delta\xi'\}\in\ell_2$, and let $\xi''$ solve the
loop with $\tau$ and $f_N$. Since $\xi'$ solves the $\tau$-loop with the input
$f+\mathcal G(\tau'-\tau)\Delta\xi'$, causality gives $P_N\xi''=P_N\xi'$. Hence
$\lVert P_N\xi'\rVert\le c_*\lVert f_N\rVert\le c_*\lVert f\rVert+c_*\sup|G|\,|\tau'-\tau|\,\lVert P_N\xi'\rVert$,
using $\lVert P_N\mathcal Gu\rVert\le\sup|G|\,\lVert P_Nu\rVert$, so $\lVert P_N\xi'\rVert\le2c_*\lVert f\rVert$ for
all $N$, and $\xi'\in\ell_2$. At $\tau=0$, $\xi=f$. Finitely many steps reach
$\tau=1$, and the a priori bound gives the claim.
head: environment

label: lem:shift
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:shift}
Let $\varrho>0$, and suppose that every trajectory $(e_k)_{k\ge-1}$ of
\eqref{eq:normrec}, with arbitrary $e_{-1},e_0$ and a fixed $\psi\in\mathcal S$, satisfies
$\sum_{j\ge0}\varrho^{-2j}\lVert e_j\rVert^2\le C_0(\lVert e_0\rVert^2+\lVert e_{-1}\rVert^2)$. Put
$C'=C_0\max(1,\varrho^{-2})$ and $\theta=C'/(1+C')$. Then
$\lVert e_k\rVert^2\le C_0\theta^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\varrho^{2k}(\lVert e_0\rVert^2+\lVert e_{-1}\rVert^2)$
for all $k\ge0$.
head: environment
name: Weighted shift

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k\ge1$ the sequence $e'_j=e_{k+j}$, $j\ge-1$, is a trajectory of the same
recursion with initial pair $(e_{k-1},e_k)$. With
$S_k=\sum_{j\ge k}\varrho^{-2j}\lVert e_j\rVert^2$, the hypothesis gives
\[
 S_k\le C_0\varrho^{-2k}\bigl(\lVert e_k\rVert^2+\lVert e_{k-1}\rVert^2\bigr)
 =C_0\bigl[(S_k-S_{k+1})+\varrho^{-2}(S_{k-1}-S_k)\bigr]\le C'(S_{k-1}-S_{k+1}).
\]
Since $S_{k+1}\le S_k$, $(1+C')S_{k+1}\le C'S_{k-1}$, that is, $S_{k+1}\le\theta S_{k-1}$
for $k\ge1$. Hence $S_{2j}\le\theta^jS_0$ and $S_{2j+1}\le\theta^jS_1\le\theta^jS_0$, so
$S_k\le\theta^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}S_0$; finally $\varrho^{-2k}\lVert e_k\rVert^2\le S_k$ and
$S_0\le C_0(\lVert e_0\rVert^2+\lVert e_{-1}\rVert^2)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varrho=e^t>r_0$, $\psi\in\mathcal S$, and let $(e_k)_{k\ge-1}$ be a trajectory of
\eqref{eq:normrec} with arbitrary $e_{-1},e_0$. The one-sided $z$-transform of
\eqref{eq:normrec} gives $e=\mathcal G_1\sigma+e^{\rm free}$, where $\mathcal G_1$ has the
transfer function $G(z)=Bz/(z^2-Az+\beta)$ and $e^{\rm free}$ is the trajectory of
$e_{k+1}=Ae_k-\beta e_{k-1}$ from $(e_{-1},e_0)$. In scaled variables,
$\tilde e=\mathcal G\tilde\sigma+\tilde f$, where $\mathcal G$ has the transfer function
$G(\varrho z)$ and $\tilde f_k=\varrho^{-k}e^{\rm free}_k$. The poles of $G(\varrho z)$ are the
roots of $z^2-Az+\beta$ divided by $\varrho$, which lie in the open unit disk since
$\varrho>r_0$; so $\mathcal G$ is stable and strictly proper, and
$\lVert \tilde f\rVert\le c_0(\lVert e_0\rVert+\lVert e_{-1}\rVert)$. Define
$\Delta:\tilde e\mapsto(\varrho^{-k}\nabla\psi(\varrho^k\tilde e_k))_{k\ge0}$. It is causal and
memoryless, and it inherits the bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:homotopy} from the
$1$-Lipschitz property of $\nabla\psi$ and $\nabla\psi(0)=0$. For $\tau\in[0,1]$,
$\tau\Delta$ is the map of $\tau\psi\in\mathcal S$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:iqc}(a) gives the
constraint for every $\tau$. Since $G(\varrho e^{i\omega})=1/m(t,\omega)$,
\[
 [G;1]^*\Pi[G;1]=|G|^2[1;m]^*\Pi[1;m]=|G|^2\Phi_t\le-\varepsilon\min_\omega|G(\varrho e^{i\omega})|^2<0
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:iqc}(b), because $|m|$ is bounded on the circle $|z|=\varrho$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:homotopy} gives
$\sum_k\varrho^{-2k}\lVert e_k\rVert^2\le c_*^2c_0^2(\lVert e_0\rVert+\lVert e_{-1}\rVert)^2\le
C_0(\lVert e_0\rVert^2+\lVert e_{-1}\rVert^2)$ with $C_0=2c_*^2c_0^2$, independent of $\psi$, of the
dimension and of the initial pair. Lemma~\ref{lem:shift}, applied to
trajectories of \eqref{eq:hb}, for which $e_{-1}=e_0$, and
$\theta^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}\le\theta^{(N-1)/2}$ give
$W_N\le(2C_0)^{1/2}\theta^{-1/4}(\varrho\theta^{1/4})^N$, so $\rho\le\varrho\theta^{1/4}<e^t$. At $t=0$, $\varrho=1>r_0$ because $|A|<1+\beta$ and
$\beta<1$; so infeasibility at $t=0$, which by
Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(a) gives a strict certificate, implies $\rho<1$.
head: environment

label: lem:symbols
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symbols}
Let $\varrho=e^t$ and $M(z)=\sum_{n=1}^N\lambda_n(1-z^n)$ with $\lambda_n\ge0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\par\hangindent 40\p@ If $t\ge0$, the weights $\alpha_n=\lambda_n\varrho^{-n}$ on $\ell_n\ge0$ and
$\gamma_-=\sum_n\alpha_n\sinh nt$ on $\bar g-C\ge0$ cancel $C$, and, with $u=e^{i\omega}/\varrho$,
the symbol is
$\Phi_t(\omega)=-\frac{\varrho^2}{B^2}|a^\sharp(u)|^2\operatorname{Re}\frac{M(u)b^\sharp(u)}{a^\sharp(u)}$.
\par\hangindent 40\p@ If $t\le0$, the weights $\alpha_n=\lambda_n\varrho^n$ on $\ell_n\ge0$ and
$\gamma_+=-\sum_n\alpha_n\sinh nt$ on $\bar g+C\ge0$ cancel $C$, and, with $z=\varrho e^{i\omega}$,
the symbol is
$\Phi_t(\omega)=-\frac1{B^2\varrho^2}|b(z)|^2\operatorname{Re}\frac{M(z)a(z)}{b(z)}$.
\end{enumerate}
At $t=0$ the two expressions agree, and on $|z|=1$ the functions
$\operatorname{Re}[Mb^\sharp/a^\sharp]$ and $\operatorname{Re}[Ma/b]$ have the same sign. For upper lags the
same holds with $a$ and $b$ interchanged.
head: environment
name: Symbols of one-sided certificates

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) The coefficient of $C$ is $\sum_n\alpha_n\sinh nt-\gamma_-=0$. Since
$\cosh nt+\sinh nt=\varrho^n$, the symbol is
$\sum_n\alpha_n\{g(\varrho^n-\cos n\omega)-2s\sin n\omega\}=\operatorname{Re}[(g-2is)\sum_n\alpha_n(\varrho^n-e^{in\omega})]
=\operatorname{Re}[(g-2is)M(u)]$. With $z=1/\overline{u}$, $a(z)=\overline{a^\sharp(u)}/\overline{u}^2$ and
$\overline{b(z)}=b^\sharp(u)/u^2$, so \eqref{eq:factor} gives
$g-2is=-\varrho^2\overline{a^\sharp(u)}b^\sharp(u)/B^2$. (b) The coefficient of $C$ is
$\sum_n\alpha_n\sinh nt+\gamma_+=0$, and $\cosh nt-\sinh nt=\varrho^{-n}$ gives the symbol
$\operatorname{Re}[(g-2is)M(z)]$, to which \eqref{eq:factor} applies directly. On $|z|=1$,
$b^\sharp(z)/a^\sharp(z)=\overline{b(z)/a(z)}=|b/a|^2\,a/b$. For upper lags $g-2is$ is
replaced by $g+2is$, which interchanges $a$ and $b$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Assume $\operatorname{Re}[Ma/b]\ge0$ on $|z|=1$. The function $F=Mb^\sharp/a^\sharp$ is
analytic on a neighborhood of the closed unit disk, $\operatorname{Re} F\ge0$ on the unit
circle by Lemma~\ref{lem:symbols}, and $F(0)=\sum_n\lambda_n>0$. By the strong
minimum principle for the harmonic function $\operatorname{Re} F$, $\operatorname{Re} F>0$ on the open
disk. For $t>0$ the circle $|u|=e^{-t}$ is compact in the open disk, so
$\operatorname{Re} F\ge\delta>0$ there, and Lemma~\ref{lem:symbols}(a) gives a strict certificate
at $t$. Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(b) gives $\rho<e^{t_0}$ for every $t_0>0$, so
$\rho\le1$. Under the strict hypothesis, the symbol at $t=0$ is negative except
at $\omega=0$, where it vanishes because $M(1)=0$. At $t=0$ and $\omega=0$,
$m=(1+\beta-A)/B=(L+\mu)/(L-\mu)>1$, so $g<0$ near $\omega=0$. Adding $\eta$ times
each of $\bar g-C\ge0$ and $\bar g+C\ge0$ adds $2\eta g$ to the symbol and keeps $C$
cancelled; for small $\eta>0$ the symbol is negative on $[0,\pi]$. Strict
certificates therefore exist at every $t\ge0$, and $\rho<1$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(b).
(b) The function $\mathsf G=Ma/b$ is analytic on $|z|>\rho_b$, so $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G$ is
harmonic on the closed annulus $r\le|z|\le1$ and nonnegative on both boundary
circles. It is not identically zero, since otherwise $\mathsf G$ would be an
imaginary constant, equal to $\mathsf G(1)=0$. By the strong minimum principle,
$\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G>0$ on $r<|z|<1$. For $t\in(\log r,0)$ the circle $|z|=e^t$ is compact in
the open annulus, and Lemma~\ref{lem:symbols}(b) gives a strict certificate at
$t$. Together with (a), strict certificates exist at all $t\ge t_0$ for every
$t_0\in(\log r,0)$, so $\rho\le r$. For upper multipliers the same argument
applies with $a$ and $b$ interchanged.
head: environment

label: prop:single
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Single-harmonic spectra

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:angle}, $g-2is=|g-2is|e^{-i\Theta}$ at $t=0$, so for one atom the
raw slacks are $|g-2is|\Lambda_n(\omega_0)$ and $|g-2is|\Lambda_{-n}(\omega_0)$, with
$\Lambda_n=\cos\Theta-\cos(n\omega-\Theta)$, and $\bar g=|g-2is|\cos\Theta$. As $n$ runs
over the nonzero integers, $n\omega_0$ runs over all nonzero multiples of $2\pi/k$
modulo $2\pi$. Hence all slacks are nonnegative if and only if
$\cos\Theta\ge\cos(2\pi l/k-\Theta)$ for every integer $l$, that is, if and only if
$\Theta\le\pi/k$. In that case $\bar g\ge0=|C|$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Take $M(z)=1-z$. On $|z|=1$, $\operatorname{Re}[(1-z)a(z)/b(z)]=H_1(\cos\omega)/|b|^2$, which is
positive for $z\ne1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic}. Theorem~\ref{thm:mult}(a) gives
$\rho<1$.
(ii) By Proposition~\ref{prop:single}, $(\delta_{\omega_0},0)$ is feasible at $t=0$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(c) with $r=1$ gives $f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^3)$ whose
trajectory is $e_N=(e^{iN\omega_0},y_N)$, the orthogonal sum of a wave in a plane
and a sequence $y_N\to0$; its distance to $x^\star$ stays above
$c\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert$, and it converges to the $k$-periodic orbit
$(e^{iN\omega_0},0)$. Suppose
$\Theta(\omega_0)<\pi/k$. Then $g_0=g(0,\omega_0)>0$, and with $C=0$ the slacks at $t=0$
satisfy $\ell_n,\upsilon_n\ge\delta_0>0$ for $k\nmid n$ and vanish for $k\mid n$. For
$t>0$ keep the atom and $C=0$. For $k\mid n$,
$\ell_n=\upsilon_n=g(t,\omega_0)(\cosh nt-1)\ge0$ when $g(t,\omega_0)\ge0$. For $k\nmid n$,
\[
 \ell_n(t)\ge\ell_n(0)+g(t,\omega_0)(\cosh nt-1)-2|g(t,\omega_0)-g_0|-2|s(t,\omega_0)-s(0,\omega_0)|,
\]
and similarly for $\upsilon_n$; the right side is positive for small $t>0$,
uniformly in $n$. Thus $(\delta_{\omega_0},0)$ is feasible at small $t>0$ with
$|C|=0<\bar g$, and $\rho\ge e^t>1$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(c).
(iii) On the closure of $\Omega_1$ relative to \eqref{eq:quad}, $\mathcal L\ge0$ on
$[-1,1]$ by continuity, so $\operatorname{Re}[(1-z)a/b]\ge0$ on $|z|=1$, and $\rho\le1$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:mult}(a). At a boundary point with $\min_\omega(\Theta-\omega/2)=0$
attained at $2\pi/K$, $\Theta(2\pi/K)=\pi/K$, so (ii) applies with $j=1$, $k=K$, and
$\rho\ge1$; hence $\rho=1$. Points of $\Omega_1$ arbitrarily close have $\rho<1$ by
(i), so the point lies on the boundary of the convergence region.
head: environment

label: lem:near1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:near1}
Assume $\Theta>\omega/2$ on $(0,\pi]$. There is $\eta>0$ with $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G>0$ on
$\{1-\eta\le|z|<1\}$. If $H_r\ge0$ on $[-1,1]$ for some $r\in(\rho_b,1)$, then
$H_{r'}\ge0$ on $[-1,1]$ for all $r'\in[r,1)$.
head: environment
name: Near the unit circle

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\mathsf G=(1-z)\gamma(z)$ with $\gamma=a/b$, which is real on the real axis,
and $\gamma(1)=x/y>0$. For $z=(1-\delta)e^{i\theta}$ with $\delta\ge0$,
\[
 \operatorname{Re}\mathsf G=\gamma(1)\delta+\Bigl(\frac{\gamma(1)}2+\gamma'(1)\Bigr)\theta^2-\gamma'(1)\delta^2
 +O\bigl((\delta+|\theta|)^3\bigr).
\]
On the unit circle $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G=(1-\cos\theta)\mathcal L(\cos\theta)/|b|^2$, and comparing the
coefficients of $\theta^2$ gives $\gamma(1)/2+\gamma'(1)=\mathcal L(1)/(2y^2)>0$. Hence
$\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G\ge\frac12\gamma(1)\delta+\frac14\mathcal L(1)y^{-2}\theta^2>0$ on a punctured
neighborhood of $1$ in the closed disk. Away from that neighborhood,
$\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G\ge m_0>0$ on the unit circle by Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic}, and by uniform
continuity also on a thin annulus inside it. For the second assertion,
$\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G$ is harmonic on $r\le|z|\le1$ and nonnegative on both boundary
circles; the minimum principle gives $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G\ge0$ on $|z|=r'$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) By Lemma~\ref{lem:near1}, the set $\mathcal R=\{r\in(\rho_b,1):H_r\ge0\}$ contains
$(1-\eta,1)$ and, with each point, every larger point of $(\rho_b,1)$. For
$r\in\mathcal R$, Theorem~\ref{thm:mult}(b) with $M=1-z$ gives $\rho\le r$; its strict
hypothesis on $|z|=1$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic}. Hence $\rho\le r_1<1$, and
$\rho\ge\rho_{\rm q}$ always, since quadratic functions belong to $\mathcal F_{\mu,L}$.
(b) If $r_1=\rho_{\rm q}$, then $H_r\ge0$ for all $r\in(\rho_{\rm q},1)$, and $H_{\rho_{\rm q}}\ge0$ by
continuity in $r$. Conversely, assume $H_{\rho_{\rm q}}\ge0$. If $\rho_a>\rho_b$, then
$\rho_{\rm q}=\rho_a\in\mathcal R$ and $r_1\le\rho_{\rm q}$. If $\rho_b\ge\rho_a$, then by
Lemma~\ref{lem:dominant} the roots of $b$ are $z_b=-\rho_b$ and $z_2\in(-\rho_b,0]$.
On the annulus $D=\{\rho_b<|z|<1\}$, $\mathsf u=\operatorname{Re}\mathsf G$ is harmonic and continuous
up to $\partial D\setminus\{z_b\}$, and $\mathsf u\ge0$ there, because
$H_{\rho_b}=|b|^2\mathsf u\ge0$ and $b\ne0$ on $|z|=\rho_b$ except at $z_b$. The residue
of $\mathsf G$ at $z_b$ is
$\varkappa=(1-z_b)a(z_b)/b'(z_b)<0$, because $1-z_b>0$, $b'(z_b)=z_b-z_2<0$ and
$a(z_b)=b(z_b)+(x-y)z_b=(y-x)\rho_b>0$. Write $z=z_b+w$. For $z\in D$,
$|z_b+w|>\rho_b$ gives $\operatorname{Re} w<|w|^2/(2\rho_b)$, hence
$\operatorname{Re}(\varkappa/w)=\varkappa\operatorname{Re} w/|w|^2>\varkappa/(2\rho_b)$, so $\mathsf u$ is bounded below
near $z_b$. Let $d_D$ be the diameter of $D$ and $\epsilon>0$. The function
$\mathsf u-\epsilon\log(|z-z_b|/d_D)$ is harmonic on $D$, tends to $+\infty$ at $z_b$, and
has nonnegative lower limits at the other boundary points; by the minimum
principle it is nonnegative. Letting $\epsilon\to0$ gives $\mathsf u\ge0$ on $D$, and
$\mathsf u>0$ by the strong minimum principle. Hence $(\rho_b,1)\subset\mathcal R$ and
$r_1=\rho_b=\rho_{\rm q}$. In both cases $\rho_{\rm q}\le\rho\le r_1=\rho_{\rm q}$.
(c) Let $\rho_{\rm q}=\sqrt\beta$. Then $\beta>0$, since for $\beta=0$ the roots are $0$,
$1-x$ and $1-y$, and $x<y$. Put $t_0=\log\sqrt\beta<0$. Both $a$ and $b$ have
complex or double roots, so $|A\pm B|\le2\sqrt\beta$, and since $B>0$,
$|A|<2\sqrt\beta$. Choose $\omega_0\in(0,\pi)$ with $2\sqrt\beta\cos\omega_0=A$. On
$|z|=\sqrt\beta$, $z+\beta/z=2\sqrt\beta\cos\omega$, so at $(t_0,\omega_0)$, $m=0$, $s=0$ and
$g=1$. With $\nu=\delta_{\omega_0}$ and $C=0$, for $n\ge1$ and whenever
$g(t,\omega_0)\ge0$,
\[
 \ell_n(t),\ \upsilon_n(t)\ge g(t,\omega_0)(\cosh nt-\cos n\omega_0)-2|s(t,\omega_0)|
 \ge g(t,\omega_0)(\cosh t-1)-2|s(t,\omega_0)| .
\]
At $t=t_0$ the right side equals $\cosh t_0-1>0$; by continuity it stays positive
for $t\in[t_0,t_0+\tau]$ with $t_0+\tau<0$. Theorem~\ref{thm:spectralgeneral}(c) gives
$\rho\ge e^{t_0+\tau}>\sqrt\beta$.

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) The values $\mathcal L(\pm1)$ are in Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic}, and both are positive
under \eqref{eq:quad}. For $\beta>0$, $\mathcal L$ is a convex quadratic with positive
endpoint values, so it is positive on $[-1,1]$ unless its vertex lies in
$(-1,1)$ and its discriminant is nonnegative; for $\beta=0$, $\mathcal L$ is linear with
positive endpoint values. On $\partial\Omega_1$, $\mathcal L$ has a double zero at $c_*$, so
$\Theta-\omega/2$ attains its minimum $0$ at $\arccos c_*$.
(b) For $\omega=2\pi j/k\in(0,\pi)$, $\Theta\le\pi/k$ if and only if
$\cot\Theta\ge\cot(\pi/k)$, that is, $\Xi(c)\ge h$ with $h=\cot(\pi/k)\sin\omega$. The
identity $\mathcal L(c)-(y-x)(1-\beta)(1+c-h)=-(y-x)(1-\beta)(\Xi(c)-h)$ gives the claim; for
$j=1$, $1+c_{1k}=h_{1k}$.
(c) By Lemma~\ref{lem:dominant}, $r=\rho_a$ is a root of $a$ in the first case, and
$-r=-\rho_b$ is a root of $b$ in the second, so Lemma~\ref{lem:Kmu} applies. If
$r=\rho_a\ge\rho_b$, every real root of $b$ is at least $-r$, so $b(-r)\ge0$ and
$K_\mu(-1)\ge0$. If $r=\rho_b>\rho_a$, every real root of $a$ is less than $r$, so
$a(r)>0$ and $K_L(1)\ge0$. Since $1\mp c>0$ on $(-1,1)$, $H_r\ge0$ on $[-1,1]$ if and
only if $K_\mu\ge0$, respectively $K_L\ge0$, on $[-1,1]$. A convex quadratic is
nonnegative on $[-1,1]$ if and only if its endpoint values are nonnegative and
either its vertex lies outside $(-1,1)$ or its discriminant is nonpositive; a
concave quadratic if and only if its endpoint values are nonnegative.
Theorem~\ref{thm:B}(b) completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) For Polyak's tuning $x=(1-q)^2$, $y=(1+q)^2$, $\beta=q^2$, $a(z)=(z-q)^2$ and
$b(z)=(z+q)^2$. With $u_0=(q^{-1}-q)/2$,
\[
 \Xi(c)=\frac{1-c^2-u_0^2}{2u_0},\quad 2u_0\bigl(1+c-\Xi(c)\bigr)=(c+u_0)^2+2u_0-1 .
\]
If $u_0\le1$, the minimum of the right side over $[-1,1]$ is $2u_0-1$, attained at
$c=-u_0$; if $u_0>1$, it is $u_0^2>0$, attained at $c=-1$. So $\Omega_1$ is the set
$u_0>\frac12$, that is, $q<\varphi^{-1}$, that is, $\kappa<\kappa_c$. At $c=-\frac12$
the right side equals $(u_0+\frac32)(u_0-\frac12)$, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:C}(b)
the three-cycle condition holds if and only if $u_0\le\frac12$, strictly if
$u_0<\frac12$; at $u_0=\frac12$ the double zero is at $c=-\frac12$, that is, at
$\omega=2\pi/3$.
(b) For $\beta=0$, $\mathcal L(c)=2(y-1)c+2-2x+xy$ is linear with positive endpoint
values, so $\Omega_1$ is the whole range. The roots are $0$ and $1-x$ for $a$, and
$0$ and $1-y$ for $b$, so $\rho_{\rm q}=\max(|1-x|,|1-y|)>0=\sqrt\beta$. If $\rho_a\ge\rho_b$,
then $r=1-x>0$ and $K_\mu(c)=r^3\{2r(y-1)c+r^2+ry-y+1\}$ is linear, with
$K_\mu(-1)=r^3(1+r)(1+r-y)\ge0$ and $K_\mu(1)=r^3\{(1-r)^2+y(3r-1)\}$; the latter is
positive for $r\ge\frac13$, and for $r<\frac13$ the inequality $y\le1+r$ gives
$K_\mu(1)\ge4r^5$. If $\rho_b>\rho_a$, then $r=y-1\in(0,1)$, $x>1-r$, and
$K_L(-1)=r^3\{3r^2+2r-1+x(1-r)\}\ge4r^5$. Thus $\mathcal Q$ is the whole range and
$\rho=\rho_{\rm q}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:B}(b).

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) At $t=0$, $\sinh nt=0$, so $C$ enters \eqref{eq:feasible} only through
$|C|\le\bar g$; if a pair is feasible, so is the pair with $C=0$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:angle}, $g-2is=|g-2is|e^{-i\Theta}$, hence
$g(1-\cos n\omega)-2s\sin n\omega=\operatorname{Re}[(g-2is)(1-e^{in\omega})]=|g-2is|\Lambda_n$ and
$g(1-\cos n\omega)+2s\sin n\omega=|g-2is|\Lambda_{-n}$, while $g=|g-2is|\cos\Theta$. The
function $|g-2is|$ is continuous and positive on $[0,\pi]$, since
$|g-2is|=|a(e^{i\omega})b(e^{i\omega})|/B^2$ and the roots of $a,b$ lie in the open
disk. So $\nu\mapsto w=|g-2is|\nu$, followed by normalization, is a bijection
between feasible probability measures and nonzero measures $w\ge0$ with
$\int\Lambda_n\,dw\ge0$ for $n\ne0$ and $\int\cos\Theta\,dw\ge0$. The curve $\Theta$
is determined by $\Xi$, whose coefficients are the three numbers in
\eqref{eq:Xi}.
(b) With $\omega=2\pi\xi/\eta$ and $\Theta=\pi/\eta$,
$\Lambda_n=2\sin(n\omega/2)\sin(n\omega/2-\Theta)=2\sin(\pi n\xi/\eta)\sin(\pi(n\xi-1)/\eta)$.
Put $\mathsf x=n\xi/\eta$ and $\delta=1/\eta\in(0,1]$. The numbers
$\sin\pi\mathsf x$ and $\sin\pi(\mathsf x-\delta)$ have strictly opposite signs if and
only if an integer $\ell$ satisfies $\mathsf x-\delta<\ell<\mathsf x$, since $\delta\le1$;
multiplying by $\eta$ gives $0<n\xi-\ell\eta<1$. The sign can change only where
one of the two factors vanishes, that is, on the lines $n\xi-\ell\eta=0$ and
$n\xi-\ell\eta=1$.
(c) At $\omega=2\pi j/k$, $(\xi,\eta)=\frac\pi{k\Theta}(j,k)$, which lies on the ray
through $(j,k)$ and satisfies $\eta\ge k$ if and only if $\Theta\le\pi/k$. Finally
$\Theta>\omega/2$ is $\xi<1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) The point $(j,k)$ lies on $n\xi-\ell\eta=1$ if and only if $nj-\ell k=1$, which
forces $n\equiv j^{-1}\pmod k$ and then determines $\ell$. The Farey relations
$bj-ak=1$ and $ck-dj=1$ show that $n=b$, $\ell=a$ and $n=-d$, $\ell=-c$ are
solutions, and since $b+d=k$ with $0<b,d<k$, these are the only ones with
$|n|<k$. The relation $bc-ad=1$ puts $(c,d)$ on the line $b\xi-a\eta=1$ and
$(a,b)$ on the line $-d\xi+c\eta=1$.
(b) For one atom at $\omega=2\pi j/k$, $n\omega\equiv2\pi r/k\pmod{2\pi}$ with
$r=jn\bmod k$, and $\Lambda_n<0$ if and only if $\cos(2\pi r/k-\Theta)>\cos\Theta$. For
$\Theta\in(0,\pi)$ and $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$, $\cos(\phi-\Theta)>\cos\Theta$ if and only if
$0<\phi<2\Theta$. Hence $\Lambda_n<0$ if and only if $0<r<k\Theta/\pi$, that is,
$r\in\{1,\dots,\lceil k\Theta/\pi\rceil-1\}$. This set is empty if and only if
$k\Theta/\pi\le1$, and for $\Theta$ slightly above $\pi/k$ it is $\{1\}$, that is,
$n\equiv j^{-1}\equiv b\pmod k$; by (a) these are the lags $b$ and $-d$ modulo $k$.

\par\hangindent 40\p@ Let $\Theta$ and $\Theta'$ be the angle functions of two tunings with
$\Theta'\le\Theta$ on $(0,\pi)$. If the conditions of
Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice}\textup{(a)} are feasible for $\Theta$, they are feasible

$\Theta(\omega)>\arg M(e^{i\omega})+\pi/2$ for all $\omega\in(0,\pi]$.

name: Monotonicity and phase floors

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Let $w$ be feasible for $\Theta$. At $\omega=0$, $\Lambda_n=0$ and $\cos\Theta=-1$; at
$\omega=\pi$, $\Lambda_n=-1-(-1)^{n-1}\le0$ and $\cos\Theta=-1$. So the restriction of
$w$ to $(0,\pi)$ is again feasible, and it is nonzero, because a measure on
$\{0,\pi\}$ has $\int\cos\Theta\,dw<0$. On $(0,\pi)$,
$\Lambda_n/\sin\Theta=\cot\Theta(1-\cos n\omega)-\sin n\omega$ and
$\cos\Theta/\sin\Theta=\cot\Theta$ are nondecreasing functions of $\cot\Theta$, and
$\cot\Theta'\ge\cot\Theta$. Hence $w'=(\sin\Theta/\sin\Theta')\,w$ satisfies
$\int\Lambda'_n\,dw'\ge\int\Lambda_n\,dw\ge0$ and $\int\cos\Theta'\,dw'\ge\int\cos\Theta\,dw\ge0$.
(b) At $t=0$ the cancellation of $C$ forces equal weights $\gamma/2$ on the two
minimizer constraints. By the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice}(a), the symbol
of the combination with weights $\lambda_n$ on the lag $n$ is
$|g-2is|\{\sum_n\lambda_n\Lambda_n+\gamma\cos\Theta\}=|g-2is|\operatorname{Re}[e^{-i\Theta}M(e^{i\omega})]$.
At $\omega=0$ it equals $-|g-2is|\gamma$, so a strict certificate has $\gamma>0$. Since
$\operatorname{Re}(1-e^{in\omega})\ge0$, $\operatorname{Re} M\ge\gamma>0$ and $\arg M\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$. For
$\Theta\in(0,\pi]$, $\operatorname{Re}[e^{-i\Theta}M]=|M|\cos(\arg M-\Theta)<0$ if and only if
$\Theta>\arg M+\pi/2$. Continuity and compactness of $[0,\pi]$ turn pointwise
negativity into the bound $-\varepsilon$.
(c) At $\omega=2\pi j/k$, each $1-e^{in\omega}$ with $k\nmid n$ equals
$2\sin(\pi r/k)e^{i(\pi r/k-\pi/2)}$, $r=jn\bmod k\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}$, whose argument
lies in $[-\pi/2+\pi/k,\pi/2-\pi/k]$; so does the argument of $\gamma>0$ and of every
nonnegative combination. For $M=1-z$, $\arg(1-e^{i\omega})=\omega/2-\pi/2$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:periodic}
Let $k\ge3$, $\omega_j=2\pi j/k$, $\theta_j=\Theta(\omega_j)$, and let $w$ be a nonzero
measure on $\{\omega_j:1\le j<k/2\}$ with weights $w_j$. Then $w$ satisfies the
conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice}\textup{(a)} if and only if
$\sum_jw_j\Lambda_n(\omega_j)\ge0$ for $n=1,\dots,k-1$ and $\sum_jw_j\cos\theta_j\ge0$.
In that case there are $f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^{2r+1})$, with $r$ the number of nonzero
weights, and $x_0$ whose trajectory converges to a $k$-periodic orbit and
stays at distance at least $c\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert>0$ from $x^\star$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\Xi(c)=q_0+q_1c+q_2c^2$, $s_\omega=\sin\omega$ and $h=\cot\Theta=\Xi(c)/s_\omega$. Since
$dc/d\omega=-s_\omega$ and $ds_\omega/d\omega=c$,
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 h'=-\frac{\mathsf M}{s_\omega^2},\quad h''=\frac{\mathsf N}{s_\omega^3},\\
 \mathsf M=(q_1+2q_2c)(1-c^2)+\Xi c,\quad \mathsf N=q_2c^4+(q_0-q_2)c^2+2q_1c+q_0+2q_2 .
 \end{gathered}
\]
From $\Theta=\operatorname{arccot}h$, $\Theta'=-h'/(1+h^2)$ and
$\Theta''=-h''/(1+h^2)+2hh'^2/(1+h^2)^2$, so
$\Theta''=(2\Xi\mathsf M^2-\mathsf N(s_\omega^2+\Xi^2))/(s_\omega^5(1+h^2)^2)$. With $A_1=-\Xi(1)$ and
$A_2=-\Xi(-1)$, that is, $A_1=-(q_0+q_1+q_2)$ and $A_2=-(q_0-q_1+q_2)$, the identity
$2\Xi\mathsf M^2-\mathsf N(1-c^2+\Xi^2)=\mathsf W/2$ is a polynomial identity in $(q_0,q_1,q_2,c)$.
This gives the formula for $\Theta''$.

Let $\omega\in(0,\pi)$ with $\Theta(\omega)\le\pi/2$, that is, $\Xi=\Xi(c)\ge0$, and
$c\in(-1,1)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:angle}, $A_1,A_2>0$, so the last two terms of $\mathsf W$
are positive. If $\Xi=0$, $\mathsf W>0$. If $\Xi>0$, then $2\Xi(1-c^2)^2>0$, and it remains
to show $F=(X-Y)^2+\Xi\mathsf L+2\Xi^2(1+c^2)\ge0$ with
$\mathsf L=X(3c+2)+Y(2-3c)$. If $|c|\le\frac23$, then $\mathsf L\ge0$. If $c<-\frac23$
and $\mathsf L<0$, then $3c+2\in(-1,0)$ and $2-3c>4$ give
$4Y<Y(2-3c)<X|3c+2|<X$; hence $X-Y>\frac34X$, $|\mathsf L|<X$, and
$F>\frac9{16}X^2-\Xi X+2\Xi^2>0$, since the discriminant $X^2(1-\frac92)$ is negative.
If $c>\frac23$ and $\mathsf L<0$, the same argument with $X$ and $Y$ interchanged gives
$F>\frac9{16}Y^2-\Xi Y+2\Xi^2>0$. Hence $\mathsf W>0$ and $\Theta''>0$.

label: lem:fan
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:fan}
Let $K\ge2$ and $k_p=pK+1$. The fractions $(p-1)/k_{p-1}<p/k_p<1/K$ are Farey
neighbors, and the Farey parents of $p/k_p$ are $(p-1)/k_{p-1}$ and $1/K$.
The points $(p,k_p)$ lie on the line $U:\eta=K\xi+1$, which is the lattice line
$-K\xi+\eta=1$ of the lag $-K$. The lattice line of the lag $mK+1$ through $(1,K)$
is $(mK+1)\xi-m\eta=1$, and it passes through $(m+1,k_{m+1})$. Modulo $k_p$,
$-pK\equiv1$ and $(p-1)K+1\equiv-K$.

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) This is Proposition~\ref{prop:periodic} with $k=k_p$.
(b) The hypothesis on $\theta_{p-1}$ requires $p-1<K+1$. Write
$\Lambda_n=2\sin(n\omega/2)\sin(n\omega/2-\theta)$. At $\omega_p$ the half angle for
$n=1$ is $\pi p/k$, and for $n=-K$ it is $-\pi Kp/k=-\pi+\pi/k$; at $\omega_{p-1}$ the
half angles are $\pi(p-1)/k$ and $-\pi K(p-1)/k=-\pi+\pi(K+1)/k$. Hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Lambda_1(\omega_p)&=2\sin\tfrac{\pi p}k\sin\bigl(\tfrac{\pi p}k-\theta_p\bigr),\\
 \Lambda_{-K}(\omega_p)&=2\sin\tfrac\pi k\sin\bigl(\tfrac\pi k-\theta_p\bigr),\\
 \Lambda_1(\omega_{p-1})&=2\sin\tfrac{\pi(p-1)}k\sin\bigl(\tfrac{\pi(p-1)}k-\theta_{p-1}\bigr),\\
 \Lambda_{-K}(\omega_{p-1})&=2\sin\tfrac{\pi(K+1)}k\sin\bigl(\tfrac{\pi(K+1)}k-\theta_{p-1}\bigr),
 \end{aligned}
\]
and the hypotheses give the four signs, since $\pi p/k$, $\pi(K+1)/k$ and all
angle differences lie in $(-\pi,\pi)$. A measure $w_{p-1}\delta_{\omega_{p-1}}+w_p\delta_{\omega_p}$
satisfies the lags $1$ and $-K$ only if $w_{p-1},w_p>0$, and then, with
$\mathsf r=w_{p-1}/w_p$, if and only if
$|\Lambda_{-K}(\omega_p)|/\Lambda_{-K}(\omega_{p-1})\le\mathsf r\le\Lambda_1(\omega_p)/|\Lambda_1(\omega_{p-1})|$.
Such $\mathsf r$ exists if and only if
$\Lambda_1(\omega_p)\Lambda_{-K}(\omega_{p-1})\ge|\Lambda_{-K}(\omega_p)||\Lambda_1(\omega_{p-1})|$, which
is $\Delta_p\ge0$ after division by $4$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:fan}, the lags $1$ and
$-K\equiv(p-1)K+1$ are two of the residues $1,\dots,k-1$, and the remaining
residues are $\{2,\dots,k-1\}\setminus\{(p-1)K+1\}$. If these are satisfied for an
admissible $\mathsf r$ and $\theta_{p-1}\le\pi/2$, then $\theta_p<\pi p/k<\pi/2$ gives
$w_{p-1}\cos\theta_{p-1}+w_p\cos\theta_p\ge0$, and (a) applies. For $p\ge3$,
$(K+1)/k<\frac12$, so $\theta_{p-1}<\pi(K+1)/k<\pi/2$.
(c) Let $p=2$, $k=2K+1$ and $\pi/k<\theta_1,\theta_2\le2\pi/k$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:farey}(b), a single atom at $\omega_j$ with phase in $(\pi/k,2\pi/k]$
violates exactly the lags $n$ with $jn\equiv1\pmod k$; for $j=1$ this is
$n\equiv1$, and for $j=2$ it is $n\equiv K+1\equiv-K$. All other lags are satisfied
by both atoms and hence by every nonnegative combination, and
$\theta_1,\theta_2\le2\pi/k<\pi/2$ gives the minimizer condition. By the formulas in
(b), $\Lambda_1(\omega_2)\ge0>\Lambda_{-K}(\omega_2)$ and $\Lambda_{-K}(\omega_1)>0>\Lambda_1(\omega_1)$,
because $\theta_1\le2\pi/k<\pi(K+1)/k$; the argument of (b), which allows
$\Lambda_1(\omega_2)=0$, shows that the program is feasible if and only if
$\Delta_2\ge0$. With $\vartheta_j=\theta_j-\pi/k$, $\pi(K+1)/k=\pi/2+\pi/(2k)$ and
$\sin(2\pi/k)=2\sin(\pi/k)\cos(\pi/k)$,
\[
 \frac{\Delta_2}{\sin(\pi/k)}=2\cos\tfrac\pi k\cos\tfrac\pi{2k}\sin\bigl(\tfrac\pi k-\vartheta_2\bigr)\cos\bigl(\vartheta_1+\tfrac\pi{2k}\bigr)
 -\sin\tfrac\pi k\sin\vartheta_1\sin\vartheta_2 .
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
The congruences are in Lemma~\ref{lem:fan}. On a $k$-periodic spectrum
$\Lambda_n(\omega_j)$ depends only on $n$ modulo $k$, which gives the coincidence of
the constraints and $D(\omega_j)=E(\omega_j)=0$. Differentiating
$\Lambda_n=\cos\Theta-\cos(n\omega-\Theta)$ gives
$\Lambda_n'=-\Theta'\sin\Theta+(n-\Theta')\sin(n\omega-\Theta)$. If $n\equiv n'\pmod k$, then
$\sin(n\omega_j-\theta_j)=\sin(n'\omega_j-\theta_j)$, so
$(\Lambda_n-\Lambda_{n'})'(\omega_j)=(n-n')\sin(n'\omega_j-\theta_j)$. With
$(n,n')=(-pK,1)$ this is $-k\sin(\omega_j-\theta_j)$, and with $(n,n')=((p-1)K+1,-K)$
it is $k\sin(-K\omega_j-\theta_j)$.

 &+\tfrac{1007042}{347985}c^2-\tfrac{92371789}{208791000}c+\tfrac{45613}{1898100} .
 \end{aligned}
